page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: When reactants are not mixed in the exact
ratio of the balanced equation, the reactant
that is completely consumed first is the
limiting reagent. It decides the maximum
steps.why: The reaction stops when one reactant runs out, so the amount of product is fixed by that reactant — not by the ones present in excess.
common_mistakes: Writing that the limiting reagent is the one present in the smaller MASS. The comparison is in moles against the equation's ratio.
Leaving out that it decides the product amount — that is why the concept exists.
steps.memory_tip: The reagent that finishes first limits the product; the leftover one is the excess reagent.
steps.margin_note: Both sentences carry weight: consumed first, and decides the product.

steps.label: The example
lines: Mixing 2 mol H₂ with 2 mol O₂: 2 mol H₂ needs
only 1 mol O₂, so H₂ is used up first.

lines.text: H₂ is the limiting reagent; 1 mol O₂ is left in excess

steps.why: A worked mole comparison shows the test: divide the available moles by the equation's coefficients, and the reactant that runs out first is the limiting one, even though the two amounts started equal.
common_mistakes: Picking O₂ because both started at 2 mol. Equal moles do not mean equal sufficiency — the equation needs H₂ twice as fast.
steps.memory_tip: Compare moles against coefficients, never moles against moles.
steps.margin_note: Any balanced reaction with a worked mole comparison earns this mark.
